title: Frontier AI Security Residency 2026 in Cambridge, UK | Fully Funded 8-Week AI Security & Cybersecurity Programme
summary: Applications are now open for the Frontier AI Security Residency (FASR) 2026 , an exciting fully funded research and engineering programme designed for individuals passionate about securing the future of artificial intelligence. Hosted in Cambridge, United Kingdom , this prestigious eight-week residency brings together engineers, researchers, and innovators to work on some of the world s most pressing challenges in frontier AI security, cybersecurity, and hardware-enabled verification. As artificial intelligence systems continue to evolve rapidly, ensuring that these technologies remain secure, verifiable, and trustworthy has become one of the greatest global challenges. The Frontier AI Security Residency provides participants with the opportunity to contribute directly to solving these complex problems while working alongside leading experts from academia, industry, and policy. The residency is fully funded, allowing participants to focus entirely on research, collaboration, and innovation without financial barriers. Residents will spend eight weeks immersed in one of the world s leading AI research communities, developing practical solutions that strengthen the security infrastructure needed for the next generation of AI systems. About the Frontier AI Security Residency The Frontier AI Security Residency is an intensive, in-person programme organized to support outstanding researchers and engineers interested in advancing AI security through cybersecurity and hardware verification technologies. The programme recognizes that AI capabilities are progressing at an unprecedented pace while security systems designed to protect these technologies are struggling to keep up. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into critical sectors worldwide, securing AI systems against misuse, cyber threats, and hardware vulnerabilities is essential. Rather than focusing on theoretical discussions alone, the residency is designed around practical engineering and research projects that directly contribute to improving AI safety and security. Participants will spend eight weeks collaborating with leading mentors, building innovative solutions, conducting cutting-edge research, and contributing to a growing global community focused on securing frontier AI technologies. Programme Details The Frontier AI Security Residency offers participants an immersive experience designed to maximize learning, collaboration, and impact. Programme Dates 12 October – 4 December 2026 Duration Eight weeks Full-time In-person Location Cambridge, United Kingdom Funding Fully funded Mission of the Residency The primary mission of the programme is to strengthen the global AI security ecosystem by supporting talented individuals working at the intersection of: Artificial Intelligence Security Cybersecurity Hardware Security Hardware Verification Compute Verification AI Infrastructure Protection AI Governance AI Policy The residency aims to support individuals who can help develop systems that verify AI behaviour, secure AI deployments, and reduce risks associated with increasingly capable frontier AI models. Why This Residency Matters Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of the security systems designed to protect it. Modern AI models are becoming increasingly powerful and are being deployed across governments, businesses, healthcare, finance, education, and numerous other sectors. As deployment expands, so does the attack surface available to malicious actors. The Frontier AI Security Residency seeks to address several important challenges, including: Verifying AI compute processes. Protecting AI models against cyber threats. Improving hardware-enabled verification. Developing trustworthy AI infrastructure. Building systems where AI security claims can be independently verified rather than simply trusted. Reducing risks associated with advanced AI capabilities. Participants will contribute directly to solving these emerging challenges while helping shape the future direction of AI security. What Participants Will Work On Residents will undertake practical engineering and research projects focused on frontier AI security. Potential areas of work include: AI cybersecurity. Hardware verification systems. AI infrastructure protection. Compute verification technologies. AI system auditing. Secure AI deployment. Security mechanisms for frontier AI. Verification frameworks. AI safety engineering. Cyber defense for advanced AI systems. Projects are designed around real-world challenges currently facing the AI security community. Learn from Leading Experts One of the most valuable aspects of the residency is direct mentorship. Participants will work closely with experienced mentors drawn from leading AI hardware companies, cybersecurity organizations, and frontier AI security teams. Mentors provide guidance throughout the residency, helping participants: Refine research questions. Develop technical solutions. Improve engineering approaches. Navigate emerging AI security challenges. Build expertise across cybersecurity and hardware verification. Residents will also attend talks delivered by leading researchers, policymakers, and experts working at the forefront of AI governance and security. Research Environment The programme emphasizes collaborative learning and interdisciplinary research. Residents will live and work together in Cambridge, creating an environment where ideas can be exchanged freely through: Daily collaboration. Group discussions. Technical workshops. Poster sessions. Mentor feedback sessions. Informal networking. Cross-disciplinary conversations. According to the organizers, breakthrough research often emerges from spontaneous collaboration, making the residential experience a central component of the programme. Build a Strong Professional Network During the residency, participants will become part of an expanding international AI security community. Networking opportunities include: Collaborating with fellow residents. Working alongside expert mentors. Engaging with partner organizations. Participating in research events. Attending expert talks. Receiving feedback from leaders in AI security. Building long-term professional relationships within the frontier AI ecosystem. These connections can continue well beyond the programme and contribute to future research collaborations and career opportunities. Benefits of the Frontier AI Security Residency Participants can expect numerous benefits, including: Full funding for the residency. Eight weeks of intensive research and engineering experience. Access to leading AI security experts. Mentorship from professionals in cybersecurity and hardware security. Opportunity to work on real-world AI security challenges. Exposure to frontier AI research. Participation in expert talks and networking events. Collaboration with a highly talented international cohort. Development of advanced technical skills. Strong professional connections within the AI security community. Who Should Apply? The residency is designed for talented individuals interested in helping secure the future of advanced artificial intelligence. The programme welcomes applicants with interests or experience in areas such as: Artificial Intelligence Cybersecurity Computer Science Software Engineering Hardware Engineering Systems Engineering Machine Learning AI Safety AI Governance Security Research Hardware Verification Computer Engineering Technical Policy APPLY HERE Applicants should demonstrate a strong interest in solving challenging problems related to AI security and verification. Application Deadline The deadline to submit applications is: 2 August 2026 Interested applicants are encouraged to submit their applications as early as possible before the closing date. Visit HERE to learn more about the Frontier AI Security Residency 2026 in Cambridge, UK Conclusion The Frontier AI Security Residency 2026 represents an exceptional opportunity for engineers, researchers, and technical professionals who want to contribute to one of the most important challenges facing artificial intelligence today. Through eight weeks of fully funded research, expert mentorship, hands-on engineering, and collaboration in Cambridge, participants will gain valuable experience while helping build the security and verification systems needed for the next generation of frontier AI. If you are passionate about cybersecurity, hardware verification, AI safety, or secure AI infrastructure, this residency offers an outstanding platform to develop your expertise, expand your professional network, and make a meaningful contribution to the future of AI security. title: Harvard Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellowship 2026–2027: Paid Opportunity for Graduate Students
summary: Applications are open for the Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellowship 2026–2027 , a paid part-time opportunity offered by the EdRedesign Lab at the Harvard Graduate School of Education. The programme is designed for Harvard University graduate students interested in educational equity, intergenerational poverty, economic mobility, racial justice and place-based systems change. Selected Fellows will work closely with nationally recognised cross-sector leaders participating in EdRedesign’s By All Means Senior Fellowship Program. Four students will be appointed for the 2026–2027 academic year. Each Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellow will serve as the primary Harvard-based liaison and strategic partner for one Senior Fellow, helping them navigate the University, develop relationships, advance projects and participate in activities across the Harvard ecosystem. The fellowship is classified in the official posting as a paid internship . Fellows will work approximately 6–10 hours per week and will be compensated at the standard Harvard graduate student rate. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, with a final deadline of 31 August 2026 . About the EdRedesign Lab The EdRedesign Lab, based at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, works to change the systems, policies and practices that shape educational and life outcomes for children and young people. Its work is guided by the belief that race, income and geographic location should not determine whether a child succeeds in school or later life. EdRedesign focuses especially on communities affected by racism, poverty and long-term disinvestment. The Lab was founded in 2014 by Paul Reville, a former Massachusetts Secretary of Education and Professor of Practice of Educational Policy and Administration at Harvard. EdRedesign supports the development of cradle-to-career, place-based partnerships that seek to improve: Educational attainment Social and emotional well-being Physical health and development Civic participation Economic mobility Access to personalised opportunities and support Rather than concentrating only on what happens inside classrooms, EdRedesign examines the broader systems surrounding children, young people and families. These systems may include local government, schools, community organisations, health services, youth programmes, social-service providers, philanthropy and employers. Why Cross-Sector and Place-Based Work Matters EdRedesign’s approach reflects the reality that many factors affecting children’s lives exist outside school. Children from kindergarten through Grade 12 spend only a portion of their waking hours in school. Their development and future opportunities are also shaped by housing, healthcare, transportation, family income, safety, community relationships, public services and access to enrichment opportunities. The Lab therefore supports strategies that move beyond isolated educational reforms. Its model combines two closely connected approaches: Place-based, cross-sector collaboration that brings institutions and community actors together to remove structural barriers and create pathways to opportunity. Relationship-based personalised support , described by EdRedesign as Success Planning, which helps individual children and young people access the services, relationships and opportunities they need. EdRedesign’s wider work involves talent development, practical research and movement building intended to influence policies, systems, public narratives and professional practice. About the Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellowship The fellowship honours Wendy D. Puriefoy, a nationally recognised leader whose work focused on school reform, civil society and community-based approaches to public education. Puriefoy served for many years as the founding President and Chief Executive Officer of the Public Education Network, which was described as the largest national network of community-based school reform organisations in the United States. Her collaboration also played an important role in the establishment of EdRedesign. The fellowship positions are supported through a partnership involving the Ford Foundation, Puriefoy’s family and other supporters. The programme was created to support Harvard graduate students committed to cradle-to-career, cross-sector work that improves outcomes for young people and families. Relationship With the By All Means Senior Fellowship Program Each Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellow will be matched with one participant in EdRedesign’s By All Means Senior Fellowship Program. The Senior Fellows are experienced leaders who have held senior positions in fields such as: Local government Public-school systems Federal government Community-based organisations Education networks Place-based partnership organisations National youth-serving organisations The listed 2026–2027 Senior Fellows are: Dreama Gentry, President and CEO of Partners for Rural Impact Elson Nash, Senior Fellow at Blue Meridian Partners and Strategic Partnerships Lead Consultant at the Education Commission of the States Christian Rhodes, Deputy Executive Director of the William Julius Wilson Institute at Harlem Children’s Zone Rey Saldaña, President and CEO of Communities In Schools National Office Sondra Samuels, President and CEO of Northside Achievement Zone Each student Fellow will support one Senior Fellow throughout the academic year. What Selected Fellows Will Gain The fellowship offers students direct exposure to senior practitioners working on complex educational, social and economic challenges. Participants will have opportunities to: Learn from nationally recognised cross-sector leaders Understand cradle-to-career place-based strategies Gain experience connecting research, policy and practice Build relationships across Harvard Support projects related to upward mobility and racial justice Strengthen programme-management and stakeholder-engagement skills Participate in senior-level meetings and events Contribute to projects affecting children, young people and families Develop practical experience in research, writing and facilitation The fellowship is not structured as a passive observation opportunity. Students will be expected to take substantial responsibility for coordination, research, relationship-building and project delivery. Main Responsibilities Serve as the Primary Harvard Liaison Each student Fellow will serve as the principal liaison between their matched Senior Fellow and the wider Harvard community. This will involve identifying faculty members, practitioners, institutes, centres and other University resources that align with the Senior Fellow’s interests and priorities. The student will help develop an engagement plan that allows the Senior Fellow to make productive use of Harvard’s academic and professional networks. Responsibilities may include: Researching relevant faculty and programmes Identifying potential collaborators Coordinating introductions Scheduling meetings Managing logistics Maintaining communication Supporting ongoing relationships Aligning proposed engagements with the Senior Fellow’s goals The Fellow must work closely with EdRedesign staff to ensure that outreach across the University is coordinated and strategically useful. Coordinate Meetings and Engagements Selected Fellows will arrange connections between Senior Fellows and relevant people or organisations within Harvard. This may involve: Preparing background information Coordinating schedules Confirming attendance Organising meeting logistics Tracking follow-up actions Supporting continued engagement Maintaining organised records Student Fellows will also help support monthly virtual office hours offered by Senior Fellows for EdRedesign partners, community members and graduate students. Provide Strategic and Administrative Support The fellowship requires students to offer both intellectual and operational support. After meetings or discussions, Fellows may be asked to turn broad ideas into practical outputs such as: Project concepts Goals Recommendations Action plans Research questions Deliverables Timelines Follow-up steps Fellows may also conduct, draft or review research relevant to the Senior Fellow’s projects. They will help manage project schedules and ensure coordination with the Senior Fellow’s chief of staff, executive assistant or other professional support personnel. Regular check-ins with the matched Senior Fellow will be required throughout the academic year. Support On-Campus Visits Each Fellow will act as the primary on-campus partner for their matched Senior Fellow during planned Harvard visits in the autumn and spring semesters. The student Fellow will help create an individualised agenda and prepare the Senior Fellow for meetings, cohort activities, presentations and other engagements. Duties may include: Developing visit schedules Preparing briefing materials Creating presentations and visual aids Supporting facilitation Coordinating public-speaking engagements Organising class visits Preparing meeting spaces Accompanying the Senior Fellow on campus Providing logistical guidance Two on-campus visits are expected, although the specific dates had not been confirmed in the posting. Contribute to Programme Design and Facilitation Student Fellows will provide thought partnership to the wider programme and may help design sessions for the full cohort. This may include: Curating content Preparing programme materials Recommending speakers or activities Designing learning sessions Supporting facilitation Contributing ideas for on-campus visits Helping improve the fellowship experience Participants will take part in both virtual and in-person activities with the cohort of Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellows. Biweekly cohort meetings are required. Promote Student-Facing Opportunities Selected Fellows will help share EdRedesign events and opportunities with Harvard students. They may use: Student organisations Academic networks Mailing lists Informal peer networks University communication channels Fellows may also contribute to other special projects undertaken by EdRedesign during the year. Required Qualifications Applicants must currently be enrolled as graduate students at Harvard University. Eligible degree categories include: Master’s students PhD students Doctor of Education Leadership students Applicants should demonstrate strong project-management skills and the ability to coordinate multiple tasks proactively. Successful candidates should be capable of: Translating conversations into practical goals Producing recommendations and next steps Managing projects and timelines Working independently between meetings Adapting when priorities change Navigating ambiguity Supporting virtual and in-person events Communicating professionally Maintaining confidentiality The role requires someone who can operate with limited supervision while remaining closely aligned with EdRedesign and the matched Senior Fellow. Knowledge of Harvard Applicants should understand the Harvard ecosystem, including its: Faculty Institutes Research centres Academic programmes Events Professional networks Students who do not already possess extensive knowledge of the University should demonstrate the ability to identify and understand relevant resources independently. This requirement is important because Fellows will be responsible for connecting Senior Fellows with people, programmes and opportunities across Harvard. Research and Analytical Skills Strong research and analytical abilities are required. Applicants should be able to collect, interpret and synthesise qualitative and quantitative information from multiple sources. Possible assignments may involve: Reviewing academic research Preparing background briefs Analysing policy documents Summarising meetings Identifying relevant programmes Drafting research materials Translating findings into recommendations Previous research experience in education, child development, economics, government or a related field would strengthen an application. Commitment to Children, Youth and Families Applicants should demonstrate a strong interest in supporting children, young people and families through cradle-to-career, place-based and cross-sector work. They must also be able to appreciate local contexts and cultures while building trusting relationships with national leaders and community partners. Experience in the following areas is considered advantageous: Collective-impact initiatives Cradle-to-career partnerships Local government Public policy School leadership Education systems Place-based collaboration Community development Child and youth development Relevant professional experience is useful, but lived experience connected to EdRedesign’s mission may also be considered valuable. Number of Positions EdRedesign plans to appoint: Four Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellows The four Fellows will form a student cohort and participate in shared learning and programme activities throughout the academic year. Fellowship Period and Weekly Schedule The programme covers the 2026–2027 academic year , including: Fall 2026 Spring 2027 The required schedule is described as flexible. Fellows are expected to work approximately: 6–10 hours per week Although the weekly schedule is flexible, participants must remain available for scheduled virtual and in-person meetings, cohort sessions, campus visits and events. Continued participation may be influenced by performance and programme needs. Compensation This is a paid position. Selected students will receive compensation at the standard Harvard graduate student rate. Funding may be provided through: Federal or institutional work-study arrangements, where eligible Non-work-study funding The posting does not state a specific hourly rate. Applicants should consult the official application information or EdRedesign for current compensation details. Work-Authorisation Requirement Applicants should be legally eligible to work in the United States. International students who are uncertain about their eligibility are advised to contact the Harvard International Office. Being an international student does not automatically make an applicant ineligible, but the student must satisfy applicable U.S. and Harvard employment requirements. How to Apply Applicants must complete the official application form and follow the instructions for submitting: A résumé A cover letter The résumé should clearly show relevant experience in areas such as: Project management Research Education Public policy Community engagement Programme coordination Student leadership Event organisation Cross-sector collaboration The cover letter should explain: Why the applicant is interested in EdRedesign Their commitment to educational equity Their interest in upward mobility and place-based work Their understanding of cross-sector collaboration Relevant research or professional experience Their knowledge of the Harvard ecosystem Their ability to support a senior leader How their skills and experiences align with the fellowship APPLY HERE Application Deadline Applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis. The final deadline is: 31 August 2026 Because applications may be assessed before the final date, interested students should apply as early as possible. Conclusion The Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellowship 2026–2027 offers Harvard graduate students an opportunity to gain meaningful experience at the intersection of research, policy, community leadership and educational systems change. Selected Fellows will work directly with prominent leaders from place-based partnerships, education organisations and community-focused institutions. They will serve as strategic partners, project coordinators, researchers, campus guides and connectors across Harvard. The programme is particularly relevant to students committed to educational equity, racial justice, economic mobility and improving outcomes for children and families. Four Fellows will be appointed for the academic year, working approximately 6–10 hours each week and receiving compensation at the standard Harvard graduate student rate. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis and must be submitted no later than 31 August 2026 . For further information and application requirements, CLICK HERE . title: British Council Springboard 2026 Research Grants: Up to £10,000 to Support International Research Collaborations Between the UK, France, Germany, and Spain
summary: The British Council has officially opened applications for the Springboard 2026 Research Grants , providing an exciting opportunity for research institutions and early-career researchers to establish strong international collaborations across Europe. The programme supports partnerships between the United Kingdom and research institutions in France, Germany, and Spain, helping research teams build long-term collaborations, increase researcher mobility, prepare competitive international funding proposals, and produce joint scientific publications. With grants of up to £10,000 , the Springboard programme serves as seed funding for collaborative activities that strengthen international academic partnerships rather than funding full-scale research projects. It places particular emphasis on supporting early-career researchers, ensuring they play a central role in building future research networks and advancing international scientific cooperation. Successful projects will begin from January 2027 , offering institutions an opportunity to strengthen their global research profile while preparing for larger funding opportunities, particularly under the Horizon Europe framework. About the British Council Springboard 2026 Research Grants The Springboard Research Grants form part of the British Council s commitment to strengthening international research collaboration and academic excellence. The programme is designed to help research teams establish sustainable partnerships between universities and research institutions in the United Kingdom and one partner country—France, Germany, or Spain. Rather than supporting large research implementation projects, Springboard provides funding that enables researchers to build relationships, exchange expertise, develop innovative research ideas, and prepare future collaborative funding proposals. The programme recognizes that successful international research partnerships require time, networking, mobility, and shared planning. By providing financial support for these activities, Springboard helps research teams lay the foundation for long-term international collaboration. Objectives of the Programme The Springboard 2026 Research Grants aim to: Strengthen international research collaboration between the UK and European research institutions. Support the professional development of early-career researchers. Promote researcher mobility across participating countries. Encourage collaborative scientific publications. Assist research teams in preparing competitive international funding proposals, particularly for Horizon Europe. Build sustainable institutional partnerships. Increase research excellence through international cooperation. Priority Research Areas Priority consideration will be given to collaborative projects that align with the thematic priorities of the Horizon Europe programme. These priority areas include: Health Culture, Creativity and Inclusive Society Civil Security for Society Digital, Industry and Space Climate, Energy and Mobility Food, Bioeconomy, Natural Resources, Agriculture and Environment Projects outside these themes may still be considered but may receive lower priority during the evaluation process. Grant Value Successful research teams may receive funding of up to £10,000 . The funding is intended to support collaborative partnership-building activities rather than financing the full implementation of research projects. What the Grant Covers The Springboard grant supports several collaborative activities that help research teams establish stronger international partnerships. 1. Springboard Team Meeting (Compulsory) Each funded project must organize a collaborative meeting involving researchers from both participating countries. The meeting is designed to: Initiate new research collaborations. Strengthen existing partnerships. Exchange scientific knowledge and expertise. Identify common research priorities. Develop future collaborative research projects. Prepare joint international funding applications. 2. Online Communication Skills Training (Optional) Early-career researchers participating in the programme may take part in optional online communication skills training designed to improve: Scientific communication. Presentation skills. International collaboration. Professional networking. Research dissemination. 3. One-Week Research Placements (Optional) Funding may also support one-week research placements at the partner institution. These placements are available for up to two PhD students from each participating country and provide opportunities to: Gain international laboratory experience. Strengthen collaborative research. Build professional networks. Enhance practical research skills. Who Can Apply? Applications are open to research teams from: Higher education institutions. Not-for-profit research institutions. Each proposal must include: One lead institution from the United Kingdom. One lead institution from France, Germany, or Spain. Although the proposal should be jointly prepared by all participating institutions, only the UK Lead Institution may submit the final application. Applications submitted by institutions outside the United Kingdom will be considered ineligible. APPLY HERE Team Composition Requirements Each application must include: A maximum of 10 participants. At least 6 early-career researchers. For this programme, an early-career researcher is defined as an individual who obtained their PhD within the last ten years. Activities Timeline Successful projects are expected to begin from January 2027 . Applicants should ensure their proposed activities align with this implementation timeline. Why Apply? The Springboard Research Grants provide numerous benefits for participating institutions and researchers. Successful applicants will have the opportunity to: Build lasting international research collaborations. Strengthen institutional partnerships across Europe. Increase opportunities for Horizon Europe funding. Publish collaborative research. Expand professional research networks. Improve international research visibility. Support the career development of emerging researchers. Gain valuable international research experience. How to Apply Applications must be submitted through the British Council s online grant platform. Applicants must first register on the platform before accessing the application form titled: Going Global Partnerships – Multi Country – Springboard 2026. Only the UK Lead Institution is permitted to initiate and submit the application. Applicants are encouraged to review the official Application Guidance document before beginning the submission process to ensure all eligibility and application requirements are met. Visit HERE to learn more about the British Council Springboard 2026 Research Grants Country-Specific Information Additional guidance is available for collaborations involving: France Germany Spain Applicants are encouraged to consult the relevant British Council country webpages for detailed information and country-specific guidance. Contact Information For additional enquiries, applicants may contact: UK–France Collaborations education@britishcouncil.fr UK–Germany Collaborations studyuk.germany@britishcouncil.org UK–Spain Collaborations education@britishcouncil.es Application Deadline Deadline: 30 September 2026 at 16:00 BST Late applications will not be accepted. Applicants are encouraged to begin preparing their applications early to allow sufficient time for institutional approvals and submission. Conclusion The British Council Springboard 2026 Research Grants offer an outstanding opportunity for higher education institutions and research organizations to build meaningful international collaborations while supporting the next generation of research leaders. By funding networking activities, researcher mobility, proposal development, and collaborative publications, the programme helps institutions establish strong partnerships that can lead to larger international research projects and increased success under Horizon Europe. Eligible institutions are encouraged to submit competitive proposals before the 30 September 2026 deadline and take advantage of this valuable opportunity to expand their international research impact. title: Belonging in Oakland: A Just City Cultural Fund 2026 Opens Applications for $300,000 Grants Supporting Artists and Community Organizations
summary: Organizations, artists, cultural practitioners, and social change leaders in Oakland now have an opportunity to secure long-term funding through the Belonging in Oakland: A Just City Cultural Fund 2026 . The initiative is accepting applications for its fourth annual funding round, offering substantial financial support to collaborative partnerships working toward racial equity, social justice, and community transformation. The program recognizes that meaningful social change happens when artists, culture bearers, organizers, and nonprofit organizations collaborate to address systemic issues affecting their communities. Rather than funding artistic work in isolation, the initiative encourages partnerships that combine creativity with civic engagement, policy advocacy, and community organizing. Through this funding opportunity, selected collaborations will receive $100,000 annually for three consecutive years , creating a total funding package of $300,000 per collaboration. In addition, participating artists and cultural practitioners will receive annual living stipends and funding dedicated to documenting their work. This initiative represents one of Oakland s most significant investments in the intersection of arts, culture, and social justice. About Belonging in Oakland: A Just City Cultural Fund Belonging in Oakland: A Just City Cultural Fund is a collaborative funding initiative designed to strengthen partnerships between artists and organizations committed to creating a more equitable and inclusive Oakland. The program is supported through a partnership involving: East Bay Community Foundation (EBCF) Akonadi Foundation City of Oakland Cultural Affairs Division The initiative also receives major financial support from the Surdna Foundation s Thriving Cultures Program . Since its establishment in 2020, the Fund has invested in projects that use arts and culture as powerful tools to address systemic inequality, amplify marginalized voices, and inspire policy and community transformation. The underlying philosophy of the Fund is that culture is not separate from civic life—it is an essential driver of social change. Grant Value and Funding Benefits Successful collaborations will receive an extensive package of financial support designed to sustain long-term impact. The funding includes: $100,000 each year Funding period of three years Total grant value of $300,000 per selected collaboration $12,000 annual living stipend for participating artists and cultural practitioners $25,000 allocated specifically for documenting the collaboration Long-term support for community-centered cultural projects Resources to strengthen partnerships between artists and organizers Support for initiatives promoting racial justice and community belonging Increased visibility for funded collaborations Opportunity to influence civic systems, policies, and community narratives The funding structure allows organizations to move beyond short-term projects and instead build sustainable collaborations capable of producing lasting community impact. Purpose of the Fund The Fund seeks projects that move beyond traditional artistic programming by combining creative expression with social justice work. Applicants are encouraged to develop projects that: Challenge harmful racial narratives Promote racial equity Create inclusive civic participation Strengthen community leadership Build equitable partnerships Develop new community structures Encourage shared decision-making Inspire policy change Foster belonging among historically marginalized communities Create lasting systems of justice and inclusion Rather than funding isolated events, the Fund prioritizes initiatives capable of producing meaningful structural and cultural transformation. History and Previous Funding Rounds Since launching in 2020, the Belonging in Oakland initiative has supported numerous innovative collaborations. First Round (2020) The inaugural funding round responded to the COVID-19 pandemic by supporting artists who helped communities imagine a more equitable Oakland during a time of crisis. Projects encouraged residents to rethink public life, civic participation, and social justice during unprecedented challenges. Second Round (2021) The second funding cycle expanded the program by supporting two-year collaborative projects focused on: Combating systemic racism Elevating marginalized voices Challenging structural inequities Promoting community-led change Third Round (2023) The most recent round funded collaborations that addressed critical community issues, including: Supporting immigrants who were formerly or currently incarcerated Advancing equitable development in Oakland Chinatown Strengthening Black cultural spaces throughout Oakland These initiatives demonstrated how partnerships between artists and community organizations can reshape public dialogue while influencing policies affecting local communities. Who Can Apply? The Fund is specifically designed for collaborative partnerships. Eligible lead applicants must be: Cultural organizations working with artists and cultural practitioners, or Social change organizations collaborating with artists and culture bearers. The lead organization must satisfy all eligibility requirements established by the Fund. Eligibility Requirements Applicants must meet the following conditions. Organizational Requirements Lead applicants must: Hold IRS-recognized 501(c)(3) status, or Hold IRS-recognized 501(c)(4) status, or Have an eligible 501(c)(3) fiscal sponsor in good standing. In addition, applicants should: Be based in Oakland Serve BIPOC communities Demonstrate experience in community engagement Show evidence of successful partnerships Have an operating budget of at least $500,000 What Types of Projects Are Encouraged? The Fund welcomes innovative collaborations that: Address racial inequities Support community healing Build civic participation Promote social justice Develop new models of community leadership Shift harmful public narratives Increase equity through arts and culture Encourage collaboration across sectors Strengthen neighborhoods Expand opportunities for historically marginalized communities Projects should demonstrate mutual benefit between artists and organizational partners while contributing toward a more just Oakland. Application Process The application process consists of two stages . Step 1: Submit a Letter of Interest (LOI) Eligible applicants must submit: Letter of Interest Organizational information Financial statements for the most recently completed fiscal year Work samples demonstrating policy change or community impact Step 2: Invitation to Submit Full Proposal After reviewing Letters of Interest, the Fund will invite up to 10 applicants to submit comprehensive proposals. Only shortlisted organizations will advance to the second stage. Application Timeline Applicants should carefully observe the following important dates. Activity Date Applications Open July 2026 How-to-Apply Webinar August 12, 2026 (11:00 a.m.–1:00 p.m. PT) Letter of Interest Deadline August 28, 2026 at 5:00 p.m. PT Awards Announced Late October 2026 Late or incomplete applications will not be considered. Required Documents Applicants should prepare: Letter of Interest Organizational profile Financial records Recent fiscal information Policy change work samples Partnership information Supporting documentation requested by the Fund Webinar for Prospective Applicants To help applicants understand the funding opportunity, organizers will host an informational webinar. The webinar will cover: Eligibility requirements Application process Required documents Selection criteria Frequently asked questions Tips for preparing a competitive application Attendance is strongly encouraged for all prospective applicants. To register for the Webinar on how to apply visit HERE Why This Grant Matters Many grant programs provide funding only for short-term activities. In contrast, Belonging in Oakland offers multi-year investment, enabling organizations and artists to build lasting partnerships. The program recognizes that cultural practitioners play an essential role in: Influencing public dialogue Building trust Promoting healing Advancing racial justice Inspiring civic participation Supporting community resilience Transforming public systems By combining financial support with documentation resources and artist stipends, the initiative creates an environment where collaborations can thrive over several years. Visit HERE to learn more about the Belonging in Oakland Organizations Behind the Initiative The Belonging in Oakland: A Just City Cultural Fund is made possible through collaboration among respected philanthropic and public institutions. These include: East Bay Community Foundation Akonadi Foundation City of Oakland Cultural Affairs Division Surdna Foundation s Thriving Cultures Program Together, these organizations seek to strengthen Oakland by investing in arts, culture, racial equity, and community leadership. Deadline Letter of Interest (LOI) Deadline: Friday, August 28, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time (PT). Late or incomplete submissions will not be accepted. Conclusion The Belonging in Oakland: A Just City Cultural Fund 2026 represents an exceptional opportunity for Oakland-based cultural organizations, artists, and social change leaders committed to building a more equitable future. By offering $300,000 in funding over three years , alongside artist stipends and documentation support, the initiative provides the resources needed to create meaningful, community-driven change. Organizations with a proven commitment to racial equity, civic engagement, and collaborative leadership are encouraged to prepare strong applications before the August 28, 2026 deadline. This funding is more than a grant—it is an investment in creative partnerships that have the power to transform communities, reshape public narratives, and build a more just Oakland for future generations. title: DLGS Call for Applications 2027: Fully Funded International PhD Scholarship in Sustainable Urban Mobility Transformations in Germany
summary: The Dresden Leibniz Graduate School (DLGS) has officially opened applications for its 2027 International PhD Programme , offering fully funded doctoral scholarships for outstanding graduates interested in advancing research on sustainable urban mobility transformations. The programme seeks innovative researchers capable of addressing some of the world s most pressing urban mobility and sustainability challenges through interdisciplinary and transformative research. Successful applicants will receive a full-time scholarship for three years , including a monthly stipend of €1,515 , together with financial support for research activities and travel. Hosted jointly by the Leibniz Institute of Ecological Urban and Regional Development (IOER) and TU Dresden (Dresden University of Technology) , the programme provides an outstanding research environment focused on spatial sustainability science and transformative leadership. About the Dresden Leibniz Graduate School (DLGS) The Dresden Leibniz Graduate School (DLGS) is an interdisciplinary graduate school jointly operated by the Leibniz Institute of Ecological Urban and Regional Development (IOER) and TU Dresden . The graduate school is dedicated to advancing research in: Spatial Sustainability Science Ecological Urban Development Urban and Regional Planning Sustainable Transformation Transformative Leadership Interdisciplinary Research Its doctoral programme encourages collaboration across disciplines to generate practical solutions for global sustainability challenges while preparing researchers for leadership roles in academia, government, and industry. Theme of the 2027 Call Levers for Sustainable Urban Mobility Transformations The 2027 call focuses on identifying innovative solutions capable of transforming urban mobility systems into more sustainable, inclusive, efficient, and resilient systems. According to DLGS, modern urban mobility systems face numerous structural sustainability challenges, including: Heavy dependence on fossil fuels Environmental pollution Negative public health impacts Accessibility inequalities Social inequity Road safety concerns Fragmented planning systems Poor integration between transport planning and land-use development While digitalization, automation, electrification, artificial intelligence, and new mobility services are transforming transportation systems at unprecedented speed, they also introduce new complexities and unintended consequences. The programme therefore seeks doctoral research capable of addressing these challenges through integrated and interdisciplinary approaches. Why This Research Matters Urban mobility is no longer viewed solely as transportation. Instead, it has become closely connected with: Urban planning Environmental sustainability Climate action Economic development Digital innovation Public governance Social inclusion Technological transformation Current planning approaches often separate transport systems from land-use planning despite their strong interdependence. Existing business models also remain dominated by traditional transport providers, while innovative mobility solutions frequently remain confined to niche applications. The emergence of spatial data science, artificial intelligence, advanced modelling, and digital technologies presents significant opportunities to rethink how cities are planned and managed. DLGS therefore encourages research capable of integrating these dimensions into comprehensive mobility transformation strategies. Key Research Gaps Identified by DLGS The programme highlights several major research gaps that applicants are encouraged to address. These include: 1. Integration of Spatial and Mobility Systems Research is needed to better understand how spatial planning and mobility interact across different geographical scales and contexts. 2. Advanced Models for Dynamic Mobility Systems Applicants are encouraged to develop models capable of analysing: Normal transport operations Disrupted mobility systems Effects of automation Effects of digitalization Decision-support systems for planners 3. Combining Data Science with Public Participation The programme seeks approaches that merge: Data-driven analytics Participatory planning Co-creation Inclusive decision-making 4. Future Scenario Development Researchers should explore mobility futures ranging from: Real-time scenarios Short-term planning Medium-term transitions Long-term sustainable futures while accounting for uncertainty. 5. Governance and Institutional Innovation The role of institutions, governance systems, and business models in enabling or limiting sustainable mobility transformations remains an important research area. 6. Inclusion of Vulnerable Groups Projects should consider how mobility systems can better serve vulnerable populations through inclusive design and evaluation. 7. Interdisciplinary Integration DLGS also identifies insufficient collaboration between disciplines such as: Transport research Spatial planning Spatial data science Urban informatics The programme seeks research that bridges these fields. Research Topics Applicants should develop doctoral projects addressing at least one of the following challenge-driven topics. 1. Public Policy Possible research areas include: Governance structures Institutional design Planning instruments Policy implementation Planning techniques 2. Business Models Potential research themes include: Sustainable mobility businesses Private-sector innovation Civil society solutions Third-sector organizations Non-profit service delivery Economic sustainability 3. Integrative Tools Projects may focus on: Data-driven approaches Analytical methods Computational models Decision-support interfaces Digital tools 4. Integrated Perspectives Applicants may also develop interdisciplinary concepts connecting: Public policy Private sector Civil society Third-sector organizations through shared methods, practices, and collaborative frameworks. Applicant Profile DLGS is looking for outstanding graduates with strong academic backgrounds and a clear research vision. Applicants should demonstrate: Academic excellence Strong analytical skills Innovative thinking Interest in sustainability research Interdisciplinary collaboration Commitment to solving complex urban challenges Eligibility Requirements Applicants must satisfy all of the following requirements: Hold a Master s degree in a relevant discipline. Have obtained their first Master s degree within the previous three years. Demonstrate above-average academic performance. Submit an original research proposal aligned with DLGS research priorities. Identify potential supervisors at TU Dresden and/or IOER. Submit all required application materials before the deadline. For projects connected to ongoing IOER activities in the Dresden/Saxony region, applicants must also demonstrate German language proficiency at C1 level . Expectations for the Research Proposal Applicants are expected to prepare an original doctoral proposal reflecting both their academic expertise and research interests. Projects may use: Qualitative research Quantitative research Empirical analysis Computational modelling Conceptual research Methodological innovation Interdisciplinary approaches are expected, while transdisciplinary research designs involving broader stakeholder collaboration are explicitly encouraged whenever feasible. Scholarship Benefits Successful candidates will receive: Full-time PhD scholarship. Funding for three years . Monthly scholarship of €1,515 . Additional financial support for: Research activities Academic travel The programme also provides access to an internationally recognized interdisciplinary research environment through DLGS, IOER, and TU Dresden. Programme Timeline Activity Date Application Deadline September 1, 2026 Programme Start March 1, 2027 How to Apply Interested applicants should prepare all required application materials and submit them through the official online application system before the deadline. Applicants are encouraged to carefully review the detailed application requirements and procedures available on the DLGS website before submitting their applications. APPLY HERE Contact Information For additional information regarding the programme, applicants may contact: Scientific Coordinator Dr. Nora Gortcheva Email: dlgs@ioer.de Visit HERE to learn more about the DLGS Call for Applications 2027 Application Deadline September 1, 2026 Conclusion The DLGS International PhD Programme 2027 presents an exceptional opportunity for talented graduates seeking to contribute to the future of sustainable urban mobility through cutting-edge interdisciplinary research. By bringing together expertise from transport studies, spatial planning, data science, governance, economics, and related fields, the programme aims to generate innovative solutions to some of the world s most pressing urban sustainability challenges. With a fully funded three-year scholarship, a competitive monthly stipend, additional research and travel support, and access to internationally recognized research institutions, the programme provides an outstanding platform for aspiring researchers committed to shaping more inclusive, resilient, and sustainable cities. Prospective applicants are encouraged to prepare a strong research proposal aligned with the programme s priorities and submit their applications before the September 1, 2026 deadline. title: Africa-Europe Youth Academy Youth Spaces Grants 2026: West African Youth Organizations Can Apply for €10,000 Grants and Up to €40,000 in Phase 2
summary: Youth organizations across selected West African countries have an opportunity to secure significant financial support to establish, develop, and strengthen spaces where young people can learn, innovate, access support, build leadership skills, and become active agents of change in their communities. The Africa-Europe Youth Academy (AEYA) Call for Projects – Youth Spaces – West Africa 2026 is inviting eligible youth organizations from Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Guinea, Mauritania, Senegal, and Togo to submit projects designed to create or strengthen safe, inclusive, accessible, and stimulating environments for young people. AEYA is funded by the European Union and implemented by Expertise France , in consortium with the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS) .
